Dokkum
dok'um
n. (town in northern Friesland; where Boniface was killed in 754, and a Reformed town of the Republic after 1580)
Frisian Dokkum, earlier Dockinga, from a personal name with the Frisian -inga, the people of Docko; the -um ending is the common Frisian contraction of -heim, a home.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Dokkum is a small walled town on the northern Frisian clay, and it is known for two things eight hundred years apart. In June 754 the Anglo-Saxon missionary Boniface, who had spent a lifetime preaching among the Germans and had come back in old age to the Frisians who had first resisted him, was killed with his companions by a heathen band near Dokkum while waiting to confirm new converts; the account is that he held up a book against the blow, and a gospel-book with a sword-cut through it was long shown as his. A church and later an abbey stood over the place. In the sixteenth century the town took the Reformation, suffered in the Frisian risings, and after 1580 was a Reformed town of the Republic with its own classis, its harbour trade, and its share in the Frisian Mennonite question. The dictionary enters it for the earlier story. Boniface was not a Reformed man and his Rome was not the dictionary's Rome; but he went where the gospel had not been preached, he went back to the hardest field when he was old, and he died with no weapon in his hand. The Reformation did not invent missionary courage. It recovered the gospel which gives such courage its only sufficient reason.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion; heathen as pagan, gentile, unconverted to Christianity; and to preach as to pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject.

expand to see more

MISSIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; a person sent by ecclesiastical authority to preach the gospel in a foreign or destitute country.

HEATHEN, n. [Sax. hæthen.] A pagan; a gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.

PREACH, v.i. [L. praedico.] To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a text of Scripture; to proclaim.

APOSTLE, n. [Gr. one sent.] A person deputed to execute some important business; particularly, one of the twelve disciples sent forth to preach the gospel.

TOWN, n. Originally, an enclosure; a collection of houses enclosed by a wall or hedge; now, any collection of houses larger than a village.

Modern Corruption

Frisian town where Boniface was killed by heathen in 754, and a Reformed town of the Republic from 1580.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is, however, a live and lazy misuse of this story in both directions. Roman writers have used Boniface to prove that the conversion of the north was papal work and the Reformation an ingratitude. Some Protestant writers have dismissed him as a papal agent, which is a sneer and not a judgment. The dictionary takes the historical record as it stands: Boniface held the doctrine of his century, including errors the Reformation afterwards named; he also carried the Scriptures to peoples who had never heard them read, and was killed for it unarmed.

The principle to recover is that the field is not chosen by the labourer's comfort. “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) was Christ's own account of the shortage, and the shortage has never been of men able to go but of men willing. An old man going back to the province that had already driven him out is a rebuke to a church that measures a call by its prospects.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek therismos (G2326), harvest; Greek ergates (G2040), a workman or labourer.

expand to see more

Greek therismos (G2326) — harvest, the act or time of reaping; “The harvest truly is plenteous”, Matthew 9:37.

Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, a field labourer; “but the labourers are few”, Matthew 9:37.

Greek leukos (G3022) — white, bright, as ripened grain; “they are white already to harvest”, John 4:35.

Greek nikao (G3528) — to conquer, to overcome; “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb”, Revelation 12:11.

Greek thlipsis (G2347) — pressure, affliction, tribulation; “we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God”, Acts 14:22.

Usage

"“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — Boniface returning in old age to the Frisians."

"“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — killed with his companions near Dokkum in June 754."

"“we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22) — a Reformed town of the Republic after 1580."
